extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classical scholars, and mathematicians/students studying Euclid and ancient geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining the definitions, proposition-types, methods (e.g., method of exhaustion), and auxiliary works (Data, On Divisions, Porisms, Pseudaria) discussed in commentary on Euclid (Books XII-XIII and related texts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'given' (magnitude, species, position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's Data defines different senses in which things are 'given': magnitude, species, and position. Examples: areas, straight lines, angles and ratios are 'given in magnitude' when we can make others equal to them; rectilineal figures are 'given in species' when the angles are severally given as well as the ratios of the sides to one another; points, lines and angles are 'given in position' when they always occupy the same place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a circle is 'given in position and in magnitude' when the centre is given in position and the radius in magnitude. The purpose of a 'Datum' is to show that, from specified givens in these senses, other quantities/relations are also 'given'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of a Datum (proposition form in the Data)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Datum (proposition in Euclid's Data) proves that if in a given figure certain parts or relations are given (in the senses above), then other parts or relations are also given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from a theorem or a problem: a Datum does not itself determine the thing (as a theorem would assert) nor direct construction (as a problem would), but establishes determinability — i.e., that the requested thing can be determined from the givens. Many Data propositions could be restated as theorems or problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification rule: theorem vs problem vs porism
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional distinctions: a theorem is proposed for demonstration of the thing enunciated; a problem is proposed for the construction (to find) of the thing enunciated; a porism occupies an intermediate position and is 'proposed with a view to the producing of the very thing proposed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus's account: porisms neither purely theorems nor problems, often stated in contracted form, and often concerned with loci; later writers sometimes mischaracterized porisms (e.g., as locus-theorems or as statements that something exists rather than produces it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data: determination of two straight lines given area and sum/difference (Data 84–85)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines contain a given area in a given angle, and if the difference (or sum) of them is given, then each of the two straight lines is determined (is 'given').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's geometric treatment is equivalent to solving certain simultaneous/algebraic relations (reduction to kx - x^2 = constant). The commentary shows the analytic reduction and Euclid's geometric solution via applying a rectangle equal to a given area and deficient by a square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data: power-of-a-point style result (Data 91–92)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle and a point in the same plane, the rectangle contained by the intercepts between this point and the points in which a straight line through the point meets the circle is also 'given'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Data-equivalent of the 'power of a point' statements (III.35–36), asserting determinability of the product of intercept lengths for any secant through a fixed external/internal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound-ratio rule (Proposition 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes which have given ratios to the same magnitude have a given ratio to one another also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally: if A:B and C:B are given ratios, then A:C is a given (determinable) ratio; used as a basic tool in Data proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for triangle 'given in species' from limited data (Props. 45–46)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a triangle has one angle given, and the ratio of the sum of the sides containing that angle (or another angle) to the third side is given, then the triangle is given in species (i.e., its shape is determined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are conditions that suffice to determine the triangle up to similarity; Data collects such determinacy criteria which are used in analysis and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure-on-line gives figure-in-magnitude (Prop. 52)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rectilineal figure given in species is described on a straight line given in magnitude, then the figure is given in magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other words, placing a figure of known shape on a line of known absolute length determines the figure's absolute size. This converts 'species' givens into 'magnitude' givens when anchored to a line of known length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle-to-area ratio criterion for triangle determinacy (Prop. 66)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a triangle has one angle given, then the rectangle contained by the sides including that angle has to the area of the triangle a given ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a fixed proportional relation linking the product of two sides to the triangle's area when an included angle is fixed — a determinacy relation used in further Data arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle-to-square-on-third-side ratio criterion (Prop. 80)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a triangle has one angle given, and if the rectangle contained by the sides including the given angle has to the square on the third side a given ratio, then the triangle is given in species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is another sufficient condition to determine the triangle up to similarity, translating a ratio involving side-products and a side-square into a species determinacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle-segment bisector determinacy (Prop. 93)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a circle given in magnitude, if a straight line cuts off a segment containing a given angle and that angle is bisected by a line meeting the chord, then: (a) the sum of the sides including the given angle has a given ratio to the chord bisecting the angle; (b) the rectangle contained by that sum and the portion of the bisector cut off outside the segment towards the circumference is also given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that chord and related segments are 'given' when the circle and segment-angle are fixed; ratios reduce to known quantities (e.g., expressions involving cosines). This is an explicit Data-style determinacy assertion for circle geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion as used by Euclid
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's method of exhaustion proceeds by constructing successive inscribed figures (e.g., prisms and pyramids inside a solid) to approximate a given figure from within and then using limit-like arguments (and lemmas such as X.1) to deduce equalities of areas/volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proof that pyramids with equal height are to one another as their bases uses iterative division into prisms and smaller pyramids, comparing sums of prisms and deriving contradictions if assumed ratios differ. The method relies on subdivision, similarity, and a reductio argument comparing sums of approximating pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' extension of exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes extended the exhaustion method by combining approximations from inside with approximations from outside — i.e., using both inscribed and circumscribed figures — compressing them until they coincide as nearly as desired with the curvilinear figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two parts of Archimedes' approach are treated separately; the exterior approximation is not merely a reduction to the interior case and plays an essential independent role in obtaining equalities for curved figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Divisions of Figures: scope and problem types
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise 'On divisions of figures' addresses dividing given figures (triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, quadrilateral, a figure bounded by an arc and two lines, circle) by straight lines into parts having prescribed ratios (including two equal parts, a given fraction, or several parts in given ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing straight lines may be transversals through vertices, points on sides, interior/exterior points, or simply parallel lines; the work includes auxiliary constructions such as 'apply to a given straight line a rectangle equal to a given area and deficient by a square' (geometric solution of equations like kx - x^2 = constant). The treatise is practical, giving constructions for many positional cases (through given points, on parallels, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Porisms: character and example locus-principle (Pappus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Porisms form a distinct class: neither pure theorems nor problems, often enunciated in contracted form, and many are loci-theorems; porisms aim 'to produce' the thing proposed and comprise principles of considerable generality and subtlety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus' example enunciation: for four straight lines cutting each other two-and-two, if three points on one line are given and the other intersection points (except one) lie on specified lines in position, then the remaining point also lies on a line given in position. A more general statement covers any number of straight lines with a triangular-number count of given intersection points. Porisms were presented as seeds of many results rather than exhaustive lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudaria (Book of Fallacies): pedagogical role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pseudaria (Book of Fallacies) enumerates fallacies and paralogisms in elementary geometry to train beginners to distinguish true inferences from deceptive ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proclus' description: Euclid set out fallacies alongside correct theorems, giving refutations and practical examples so learners could practice identifying errors; the work served as an exercise/catharsis complementary to the Elements' rigorous theory.
